source.title: Representation Bending for Large Language Model Safety
source.authors: Ashkan Yousefpour; Taeheon Kim; R. Kwon; Seungbeen Lee; Wonje Jeung; Seungju Han; Alvin Wan; H. Ngan; Youngjae Yu; Jonghyun Choi

page_placements.theme: Behaviour analogue: refusal/safety training and harmful-behaviour unlearning undone by fine-tuning, ablation, priming and jailbreaks

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some extracted figures and tables contain garbled or flattened text, but the relevant reported results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates safety fine-tuning methods under jailbreak attacks and reports whether fine-tuning RepBend again on unsafe data can restore harmful behavior. It does not test the claim’s targeted-knowledge accuracy or compare recovery against a model that never learned the knowledge.
record.gate_note: Rows cover reported jailbreak attack-success rates (ASR) and the qualitative unsafe-data relearning result. The paper also reports capability and over-refusal results, representation visualizations, other jailbreak evaluations, and per-benchmark results for additional methods; those are not rows for these claim versions or are omitted as described below. Hyperparameter-selection values and cited findings are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: RepBend is a safety fine-tuning method. The paper measures harmful-request compliance (jailbreak ASR), over-refusal and general capability, not accuracy on targeted knowledge. Unlearning methods (RMU, NPO, TA, WHP) appear only as safety baselines. The relearning remark is a qualitative limitation about harmful content, with no numbers. No result bears on whether forgotten knowledge is deleted or recoverable, so the ASR findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that RepBend cuts jailbreak ASR by up to 95%, beating Circuit Breaker, RMU, NPO and TA, with negligible capability loss. In Limitations they note it can relearn harmful content when fine-tuned on unsafe data.
record.recipe_differences: RepBend is a representation-bending safety fine-tuning method, trained with LoRA and safe/unsafe examples. The paper does not reproduce the cited targeted-knowledge unlearning methods or test the original claim's targeted-knowledge accuracy measure.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack access type and benchmark condition change reported ASR. The authors also report sensitivity to hyperparameters and target layers, but those ablations are not recovery tests for these claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: RepBend lowers average jailbreak ASR to 3.25 (Mistral) and 3.13 (Llama3). The original models score 60.64 and 34.00. Safety-trained RMU, NPO, CB and TA keep substantial white-box ASR; Llama3 NPO reaches 51.67 under Input Embed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation-level safety fine-tuning resists white-box jailbreaks better than output-level unlearning baselines (refusal behaviour, not knowledge removal).

fits_no_version.finding: Table 8, Llama3: weight orthogonalization restores harmful compliance for NPO (76.88 vs original 80.31 on HarmBench) but not for RepBend (5.94). CB* reaches 33.75.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-direction ablation undoes NPO safety training almost fully but not representation-bending training (an analogue of C for refusal behaviour).

fits_no_version.finding: The authors state that RepBend fine-tuned on unsafe data relearns harmful content. No numbers are given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation-bending safety training is not robust to harmful fine-tuning.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL), 2025
record.problems: The central evaluations measure harmful-response compliance on safety and jailbreak benchmarks, not targeted-knowledge recall. The original model is a comparison but is not a model that never learned the knowledge. The relearning result is qualitative and lacks reported data size, model-specific details, and quantitative results. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: To stay within the 60-row limit, individual benchmark ASRs for Task Arithmetic, RMU, Circuit Breaker, and the public safety-tuned comparators in Table 1 are omitted; their aggregate results are included where selected. Additional attack results in Tables 8-10 and the separately reported capability and over-refusal metrics are also omitted because they do not add the selected prompt-recovery outcomes or are not directly tests of these versions.

untested.parts: No targeted-knowledge accuracy (e.g. WMDP) is measured for any method.
No quantitative relearning experiment. Only a qualitative remark that unsafe-data fine-tuning relearns harmful content.
No ablation restoring forgotten knowledge. Weight orthogonalization is applied to refusal behaviour only.
Jailbreaks target harmful compliance, not recall of unlearned knowledge.
RepBend's robustness claim concerns refusal under jailbreaks, not resistance of unlearned knowledge to recovery attacks.

record.verdict_notes: This is a safety and refusal paper. Its 'unlearning' baselines are trained on harmful prompt/response data for refusal, not on a knowledge forget set. None of the ASR rows measures recovery of deleted knowledge, so the reader's B/E/F labels are removed. r17 has a minor discrepancy: 3.25 in Table 1 vs 3.24 in Table 2.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports safety compliance and general-capability measures, not targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance together with simple-attack recovery compared with a model that never learned the knowledge.
The unsafe-data fine-tuning result is qualitative; the size of the relearning set and whether it was unrelated, loosely related, or a subset of forgotten facts are not stated.
No activation-direction ablation is reported, and the representation analysis does not establish that knowledge is blocked from access rather than deleted.
The study tests jailbreak attacks, not prompt rephrasing in general or other languages. It does not compare attack success with a never-trained knowledge control.
RepBend is evaluated on jailbreak attacks and the authors report qualitative relearning after unsafe-data fine-tuning; quantization and activation-ablation resistance are not tested.

rows.subject: R EP B END
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned the method with unsafe data after safety training; authors report that harmful content can be relearned.

conditions.value: unsafe data; size and exact composition not stated

rows.measure: Authors' qualitative statement that the model can relearn harmful content.
rows.baseline: not stated
rows.value: Can relearn harmful content when fine-tuned with unsafe data.
rows.note: The text attributes this finding to the authors' own experiments but gives no numerical result, model-specific result, or fine-tuning set size.
rows.check: A one-sentence limitation, with no numbers, data size or model. It concerns relearning harmful behaviour, not hidden targeted knowledge. Too thin to be a result row.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The paper uses unlearning methods (RMU from the WMDP original, NPO) as baselines and does not test whether knowledge unlearning is shallow. Its relearning remark in Limitations is qualitative, about harmful content.

tranche.reason: RepBend is a safety fine-tuning method. It measures jailbreak ASR, over-refusal and capability, not targeted-knowledge accuracy (no WMDP). RMU and NPO are only safety baselines, and the authors report their own method's performance.

source_check.notes: No rows or verdicts are listed. Table 8 (weight orthogonalization) measures harmful compliance, not knowledge, so it fits no version (as the unfit theme records). Limitations states only in words that RepBend relearns harmful content when fine-tuned on unsafe data. Tables 1 and 8 are flattened in the text, but the column order can be read.

statements.correction: Table 8 (App. B.2), Llama3 8B Instruct, weight orthogonalization attack, HarmBench ASR: Original 80.31, NPO 76.88, CB* 33.75, RepBend 5.94. WildGuardTest: 82.64, 81.04, 30.95, 7.48. NPO Llama3 average ASR without attack: 10.62 (Table 2).
statements.problem: None. Numbers match Table 8 (Llama3 8B Instruct, HarmBench ASR under weight orthogonalization). 80.31 is Original Weight under the same attack. Table 8 has no unattacked NPO row, but Tables 1-2 give NPO low ASR without attack, so 'restores' is fair.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The authors state that unsafe-data fine-tuning can relearn harmful content (r59); set size and relation to forgotten examples are unspecified.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Jailbreak evaluations reported for RepBend and selected unlearning comparators
reader_labels.reason: Attack compliance is generally far below the original-model aggregate, but is nonzero in several settings and varies by attack; this is not a test of every prompting strategy or against a never-trained knowledge control (r01-r18, r22-r24, r34-r36, r43-r58).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: RepBend on the reported black-box and white-box jailbreak benchmarks
reader_labels.reason: Reported RepBend ASRs are low across the tested attack sets relative to the original-model aggregate rates (r01-r18).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that unsafe-data fine-tuning can relearn harmful content, so robustness does not extend to that retraining condition (r59).
